questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a co-movement between two series establishes
questions.stem: In one port the number of ships arriving and the number of grain price rises both climb across the same thirty years. What can that pairing establish?

options.text: That the two moved together, without settling what linked them
That more arrivals caused the price rises of the following winter
options.misconception: treats co-movement in time as a demonstrated mechanism

options.text: That both trends came from a single shared cause already known
options.misconception: invents a common cause for which there is no evidence

options.text: That the price rises must have been caused by the growth in trade
options.misconception: makes one of two co-moving series the cause of the other

questions.explanation: Two series that rise together are a single observation, and a third thing such as demand, war, weather, or debased coin could be driving both, so the pairing licenses a question rather than an answer. The tempting options pick a direction and a mechanism out of a coincidence of timing, supply a shared cause no source names, and rule out the possibility that a third factor is doing all the work.
questions.hint: How many explanations does one co-movement leave open?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish co-occurrence from necessity and sufficiency
questions.stem: Every year the harbor froze and every year the salt tax was waived. What has this record established about the freezing and the waiver?

options.text: Freezing was regular, which is not the same as being the cause
That the freeze was sufficient on its own to cause the waiver
options.misconception: reads a perfect pairing as a complete explanation

options.text: That the waiver was needed whenever the harbor froze
options.misconception: inverts the pairing into a requirement of the second for the first

options.text: That without a freeze the waiver would never have happened
options.misconception: turns a recurring combination into a counterfactual claim

questions.explanation: A regular pairing shows only that the two went together in the years recorded, and from that it does not follow that the freeze alone produced the waiver, since the practice may have rested on the expectation of a freeze rather than on each year's freeze. The tempting options read sufficient, necessary, and counterfactual claims out of a pattern that establishes co-occurrence and nothing beyond it.
questions.hint: What can a repeated pairing prove about one case?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: separate the triggering event from the longer process behind it
questions.stem: A revolt begins the day a grain shipment is cancelled, and the price had been falling for a year before that. Which reading of cause is soundest?

options.text: The cancelled shipment is the trigger on a longer downward trend
The falling price is the cause, since the shipment came afterwards
options.misconception: orders causes by importance rather than by time

options.text: The shipment is the whole cause, and no earlier condition matters
options.misconception: lets the nearest event swallow the longer process behind it

options.text: The price caused the revolt, and the shipment merely followed it
options.misconception: reverses the sequence and then discards the trigger

questions.explanation: Causal language has to say which thing is claimed to do what, and here a year of falling prices is a condition that made a cancellation intolerable while the cancellation is the event that set the revolt going, so a sound account keeps both with distinct jobs. The tempting options sort causes by how interesting they are, hand the entire explanation to the nearest event, or reverse the order and then throw away the trigger.
questions.hint: Which event set it off, and what made it go off?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Timing as a test of a causal claim
questions.learningObjective: test a causal claim against the timing of the series it invokes
questions.stem: A harbor's grain price index reads 100 in the 1380s, 112 in the 1390s, and 118 in the 1400s before a grain tax is set in 1402, then 121 in the 1410s. What does the sequence show?

options.text: The rise began well before the tax, so timing does not support it
That the tax caused the rise, since the rise continued afterward
options.misconception: accepts continuation after an event as proof the event caused it

options.text: That the rising price caused the tax, being set to relieve it
options.misconception: inverts cause and effect because relief logically follows harm

options.text: That the index measures a tax effect alone, with nothing else in it
options.misconception: assumes one cause behind a series that predates the tax

questions.explanation: Eighteen of the twenty-one index points, 86 percent of the total rise, are already on the books before the tax is enacted, and the decade after it adds only three, so the sequence cannot carry a claim that the tax drove the rise. The tempting options read continuation as proof of causation, invert the pair because relief logically follows harm, and treat the series as a pure measure of the tax's effect.
questions.hint: How much of the rise predates the tax?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify the confounding factor a two-variable explanation ignores
questions.stem: In a province, guild membership rose and literacy rose, and towns that joined guilds built more schools. What should be asked before literacy explains the schools?

options.text: Whether richer towns caused both membership and school building
Whether the guilds themselves required members to read
options.misconception: accepts the first convenient link without testing an alternative

options.text: Whether schools were counted only in guild towns by the recorders
options.misconception: takes a boundary in the data for a fact about the world

options.text: Whether the province's schools were older than its guilds
options.misconception: checks chronology only where it cannot matter

questions.explanation: Whenever two things rise together the useful question is what moved them both, and a town's wealth would make membership attractive and a school affordable at once, so the pair needs a candidate for the third term before either can be called a cause. The tempting options settle for the first link that sounds plausible, blame the boundary of the records, and check the one relation that chronology cannot settle.
questions.hint: What would make one town do both things?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify a change that removed a limit rather than produced a new event
questions.stem: A harbor's dredged channel let larger ships in, and the customs house had already moved its offices before the dredging began. What role was the dredging playing?

options.text: A condition that removed a limit on an existing trade
The cause of the customs house's decision to move
options.misconception: makes a later capacity a reason for an earlier choice

options.text: Proof that trade had collapsed before the channel was dug
options.misconception: reads a later improvement as proof of a prior collapse

options.text: The whole explanation, leaving the earlier office move unexplained
options.misconception: hands every effect to the single change named last

questions.explanation: A channel answers to the trade that was already there, and the customs house moved first, so the dredging removed a ceiling on a volume the office had already committed itself to expecting. The tempting options turn capacity into a reason for the earlier move, read the new depth as evidence that the old trade had died, and leave the earlier decision with no explanation at all.
questions.hint: Which came first in the record?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a policy's stated aim from its measured result
questions.stem: A ministry abolished a guild's inspection regime to spare bakers harassment, and within a decade the quality of city bread fell. What does the pair show?

options.text: A stated aim and a measured outcome that run in opposite directions
That the ministry intended the decline in bread quality
options.misconception: reads an unintended result as a concealed purpose

options.text: That the inspectors had secretly been protecting their customers
options.misconception: credits the old regime with the ministry's own stated concern

options.text: That the guild caused the decline to prove the reform necessary
options.misconception: assigns the bad outcome to the party that opposed reform

questions.explanation: Policy is judged by the gap between what a ministry says it wants and what the years afterwards show, and here the declared aim was relief while the record of the bread shows decline, which makes the outcome evidence about the policy rather than about its motive. The tempting options reverse motive and result, credit the abolished regime with the ministry's own concern, and blame the guild for the harm that justified the reform.
questions.hint: Separate what was meant from what followed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: combine a dated shock with a slow trend in one account
questions.stem: A monsoon failure is recorded in one chronicle as a single dry year, while a settlement record shows the same region's wells already shallow for a decade. Which reading best fits both?

options.text: A short shock inside a slow weakening of the same structure
The chronicle is wrong, since the failure was really a long process
options.misconception: collapses a dated event into the trend that surrounded it

options.text: The two describe unrelated events that happened to share a region
options.misconception: severs an event from the conditions that shaped it

options.text: The wells prove the wells, and the drought proves the drought
options.misconception: mistakes two descriptions of one thing for one claim twice

questions.explanation: The chronicle registers what a person felt as a single break while the settlement record measures a slow loss of capacity beneath it, and both can be true because an event inside a weakening structure is exactly what two such records would show. The tempting options dissolve the dated event into the trend, cut the event off from the conditions that shaped it, and mistake two descriptions for a single claim repeated.
questions.hint: Can a break sit inside a decline?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state what a persistent practice supports about continuity
questions.stem: Landholding rules in a region are recorded in similar terms in the 1100s and again in the 1600s. What does that similarity support?

options.text: That a durable arrangement survived many changes around it
That nothing in the region's economy altered across six centuries
options.misconception: extends one stable feature to everything else

options.text: That the earlier rules were copied without any later change
options.misconception: reads surviving form as proof of untouched content

options.text: That similar words mean similar institutions in both centuries
options.misconception: assumes identical vocabulary guarantees identical practice

questions.explanation: Continuity is a claim about a specific arrangement holding while much else changes, and the same terms recorded six centuries apart is evidence of durability for that arrangement, not of a static society. The tempting options extend the stability to the whole economy, treat surviving wording as unchanged substance, and assume that matching language guarantees matching practice underneath it.
questions.hint: How much else changed in those six centuries?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: hold continuity and change together in one account
questions.stem: A region's village council keeps the same offices, oaths, and meeting seasons for four centuries while the tax rolls it assesses grow fivefold. Which synthesis holds both facts?

options.text: The forms endured while the material base of the village shifted
The forms are unchanged, so the village cannot really have grown
options.misconception: lets institutional naming bar any economic change

options.text: The rising rolls show the offices were abolished and rebuilt
options.misconception: invents a constitutional rupture to explain a tax series

options.text: The council kept its forms because the village had no new problems
options.misconception: reads unchanged procedure as an absence of new difficulties

questions.explanation: Institutions are often the part of a society that outlives a change in the scale of its economy, and a council can keep its oaths and seasons while the wealth it assesses multiplies, which is why continuity and change have to be stated about different things. The tempting options let the stable names cancel the rising rolls, invent an abolition to explain growth, and read unchanged procedure as an absence of new problems.
questions.hint: Name the thing that changed and the thing that did not.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify the test a progress narrative must pass
questions.stem: A chronicle presents a century of reform as a straight road from darkness toward order. What should a historian check first?

options.text: Whether the reform's victims and costs are recorded anywhere
Whether the reforms were large enough to fill a century
options.misconception: measures a period by the volume of its legislation

options.text: Whether earlier chronicles also called their own age dark
options.misconception: accepts the gloom of a source as evidence about the age

options.text: Whether the same reforms could be repeated today
options.misconception: tests a period by the feasibility of a modern program

questions.explanation: A progress narrative claims that the whole interval was an improvement, and such a claim has to be tested against what the reform cost and who bore it, since a rising series of ordinances says nothing about the harvest or the wage of those it moved. The tempting options measure the period by its legislative volume, accept a source's gloom as evidence of darkness, and judge the century by whether its program would still work.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain what a disagreement over period boundaries turns on
questions.stem: One historian ends his chapter at 1500 and the next begins his at 1492. What does their disagreement turn on?

options.text: Which break each thinks deserves the foreground of the story
Which of the two has read more printed books this year
options.misconception: settles period boundaries by counting the reading behind them

options.text: Which side was in fact more important to later writers
options.misconception: defers the boundary to later fame rather than to the argument

options.text: Which date is easier to remember and repeat in a lecture
options.misconception: chooses a boundary for its convenience as a spoken label

questions.explanation: A period boundary is an argument about which change the story should turn on, so two historians can both be right about their facts and still draw the line in different places, each foregrounding a different break. The tempting options reduce the disagreement to reading load, to later reputation, and to the convenience of a memorable label, none of which is the reason a boundary is chosen.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: justify comparing two separate regions that changed alike
questions.stem: Two regions four thousand kilometers apart both shift from labor services to cash rents within fifty years. Which claim about them is best supported?

options.text: Both shifts followed pressures that were common to both regions
That the two regions copied each other's land tenure
options.misconception: assumes direct contact where the timing only coincides

options.text: That one region's change came first and caused the other's
options.misconception: reads a similar timing as proof of transmission

options.text: That the change came from a single law made in one capital
options.misconception: invents a common legislature for two unconnected regions

questions.explanation: Independent regions moving the same way at the same time is evidence for a shared pressure, such as a labor supply that no longer answered to coercion and money rents that households could actually pay, and comparison is the only warrant for treating them together. The tempting options invent contact, transmission, and a common legislature, each of which adds an actor the record never provides.
questions.hint: What can explain two separate places at once?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: design a test separating a contingent outcome from a patterned one
questions.stem: A regime fell when a single officer was dismissed. Which finding would show the fall was not a contingency?

options.text: The same collapse follows that officer in three other regimes
That the officer held the office for a very short time
options.misconception: judges causal weight by how long a man was in post

options.text: That the officer had enemies among the court's own families
options.misconception: explains the outcome by a motive rather than a pattern

options.text: That the regime was poor when the officer arrived
options.misconception: treats a general condition as a specific explanation

questions.explanation: A contingent outcome is one that turned on a single person, and the way to test that is repetition, because if the same dismissal ends three other regimes the officer was part of a pattern rather than a hinge. The tempting options measure the hinge by length of service, explain the fall by a motive, and settle for a general poverty that was equally true of a hundred regimes that did not fall.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: explain the flaw of reading a later outcome into an earlier decision
questions.stem: A historian writes in 1930 that a war 'led to' a revolution, and the revolution comes eleven years later. What has gone wrong in the reasoning?

options.text: The later outcome is being read back into the earlier decision
That the two events cannot be connected at all, being decades apart
options.misconception: decides no connection is possible whenever the gap is long

options.text: That the war leaders secretly intended the revolution
options.misconception: supplies a motive no document records for anyone in 1930

options.text: That a revolution only follows wars that were lost
options.misconception: states a law from a single case with no basis offered

questions.explanation: A causal claim is made from the vantage of what followed, and here the revolution is the very thing the historian is trying to explain, so treating it as the outcome of 1930 explains nothing and assumes the ending in advance. The tempting options forbid long connections, supply a secret intention for actors who could not have had it, and elevate one case into a general law about how wars end.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: identify what a character trait leaves out of a causal account
questions.stem: A tax rebellion is explained by saying that the collectors were cruel. What does that explanation leave out?

options.text: Why the collectors were pressed to work that way at all
That the collectors were not cruel in their private conduct
options.misconception: replaces a structural account with a remark about private character

options.text: That the rebellion failed, since the collectors stayed in place
options.misconception: borrows an outcome as evidence for a cause already given

options.text: That cruelty appears in every rebellion of the period
options.misconception: assumes a general regularity from a single instance

questions.explanation: A character trait explains a mood but not a system, and cruelty that is routine in a collection office is usually produced by quotas, distance, and weak oversight, so a fuller account asks what the collectors were required to achieve. The tempting options shift the explanation onto private conduct, borrow the rebellion's failure as support for the cause already given, and generalize one case into a regularity.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: decide what a set of ledgers can and cannot rank
questions.stem: A harbor's ledgers show a dues reform in 1504, a shift to bigger crews in 1510, and a new market charter in 1520. Which contributed most to the growth that followed?

options.text: Cannot be settled from these ledgers, which record only dues
The charter of 1520, being closest in time to the growth
options.misconception: ranks causes by proximity to the effect rather than by evidence

options.text: The crew change of 1510, since crews moved more cargo by hand
options.misconception: picks the mechanical explanation because it sounds concrete

options.text: The reform of 1504, being the earliest of the three changes
options.misconception: assumes the earliest change must carry the greatest weight

questions.explanation: Weights cannot be read off a chronology, and a book that records dues only cannot tell the analyst whether the crews, the charter, or something outside the ledgers did the work, so the honest answer is that these sources cannot rank the three. The tempting options rank by closeness in time, choose the most mechanical-sounding cause, and assume the earliest change must be the deepest, none of which is evidence of contribution.

questions.learningObjective: select the evidence that discriminates between rival explanations
questions.stem: Two studies disagree on why a port peaked and then emptied: one blames a rival harbor's deep-water quay, the other blames the exhaustion of nearby woodland fuel. Which step best settles it?

options.text: Compare ship sizes and fuel prices around the years of the peak
Count how many studies each side has published since
options.misconception: decides a dispute by the size of the literature on each side

options.text: Ask which explanation makes the better story for a reader
options.misconception: chooses the account with the greater narrative appeal

options.text: Assume both were causes, since two factors are always enough
options.misconception: keeps every candidate because adding causes risks nothing

questions.explanation: Competing explanations are settled by a measure each of them predicts differently, and here the rival quay predicts a change in the size of ships that could enter while the fuel shortage predicts a change in the price and origin of fuel, so one dated series bears on both. The tempting options settle by counting publications, by literary appeal, and by keeping every candidate, none of which tests anything.

questions.learningObjective: read an out-of-order pair as codification of an existing practice
questions.stem: A guild wage board is sealed in 1485, yet a minute from 1479 already records a fixed rate of eight shillings for the same craft. What does the order show?

options.misconception: reverses the rule that fixes which practice is older

options.misconception: uses a later payment to deny an earlier recorded act

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a structural condition from a discrete event
questions.stem: Coastal shipping, plague, and the labor regimes of a region all press on the same two centuries. What kind of causes are these?

options.text: Coincidental features that happen to fall in the same century
options.misconception: dismisses a shared span of time as mere coincidence

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: state the test a proposed turning point must pass
questions.stem: A single battle is dated 1415 and described as the point where everything changed. What should a historian ask about such a date?

options.text: Whether the change ran in both directions around that year
Whether the battle was fought on the correct calendar day
options.misconception: checks a date's precision instead of its explanatory weight

options.text: Whether later writers chose 1415 because it sounded like a year
options.misconception: treats a popular choice of year as the cause of the change

options.text: Whether the battle's commanders had written their memoirs
options.misconception: looks for a memorial source rather than for change in the record

questions.explanation: A turning point is a claim about the shape of a curve, and the test is whether the change runs before it as well as after it, since a date that merely sits on a slope changes nothing. The tempting options check the calendar, blame later writers for liking the year, and look for a memoir as though the existence of a narrative settled the shape of the series.
questions.hint: Did the curve break at that year?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: frame the right question for an event that did not happen
questions.stem: A port with deep water and ample coal never built a shipyard within forty years. Which question is the most useful one to ask?

options.text: Who controlled the money and the shoreline where one would stand
That the port was rich, so a yard was never needed
options.misconception: treats prosperity as a reason to skip a capability

options.text: That the technology did not yet exist anywhere in the world
options.misconception: supplies a global absence no record in the case could establish

options.text: That the crewmen refused the work, as other ports report
options.misconception: borrows an explanation from a report about a different place

questions.explanation: A non-occurrence is explained by the conditions that kept it from happening, and here the useful inquiry is the control of the money and of the shoreline, since a yard needs a specific stretch of bank and a specific payer. The tempting options treat wealth as a reason not to need a yard, invent a world-wide absence of technology, and import a report about a different port's labor.
questions.hint: What would someone have had to own first?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: rank a crisis's elements by distance from the event
questions.stem: Four elements of one crisis are listed. Which order runs from the most distant cause to the most immediate?

options.text: The trade route shifted away a generation earlier
options.misconception: puts the most distant pressure at the immediate end

options.text: Rulers then raised tolls on the remaining route
options.misconception: treats a policy decision as less immediate than a harvest

options.text: Two poor harvests cut the town's income
options.misconception: places the sharpest shock at the distant end

options.text: A food riot emptied the market square in March
options.misconception: puts a single day's event below the conditions behind it

questions.explanation: Ranking by immediacy sorts a crisis by how many steps separate each element from the event, so the shift in the route sits a generation back, the tolls follow as a policy response, the harvests bite next, and the riot is the day itself. The tempting orders promote the harvest or the riot to the structural end, and treat a deliberate policy as less immediate than weather, inverting both distance and responsibility.
questions.hint: How many steps sit between each and the day itself?

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: order a chain so that no step is the result of a later one
questions.stem: A harbor's decline is traced through five steps. Which order makes the argument coherent?

options.text: New competitors build deeper harbors on the same coast
options.misconception: treats a distant development as the final link in the chain

options.text: Ships grow larger than the old harbor's channel allows
options.misconception: makes a physical limit appear before anything caused it

options.text: The old harbor's dues cannot compete and fall away
options.misconception: makes an income decline the cause of the rerouting behind it

options.text: Cargoes shift to the rival harbors each season
options.misconception: puts the market's response before the limit that moved it

options.text: Owners stop investing in dredging the channel
options.misconception: reverses the neglect and the restriction that followed it

questions.explanation: A chain argument holds only if each step produces the next and none is a consequence of a later one, and here the rival harbors and the deeper-draught ships create the constraint, deferred dredging turns it into a closure, cargo follows the constraint, and the dues fall last because the cargo has already gone. The tempting orders put the constraint after the neglect, the market's response before the limit that moved it, the income decline before the rerouting that caused it, and the deepest development at the end.
questions.hint: No step may be the result of a step below it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: assess which use of several periods makes an argument strongest
questions.stem: A student claims that waterworks explain a city's fall, and the record offers three periods. Which use of them makes the argument strongest?

options.text: Three periods showing the same mechanism, with one exception examined
Three periods in which waterworks are mentioned without any analysis
options.misconception: accumulates mentions and treats repetition as demonstration

options.text: Three periods in which waterworks are shown to be the only variable
options.misconception: claims a single cause and never counts a rival factor

options.text: Three periods chosen because each one confirms the claim in advance
options.misconception: confirms the thesis by selecting only supporting cases

questions.explanation: A thesis over several periods is carried by a mechanism that recurs in all of them and by a willingness to look at the one period where it fails, because an account that survives its exception is doing more than collecting agreeing cases. The tempting options repeat mentions, insist on a single variable with no rival ever counted, and select periods for confirmation, which is the method that would hide a counterexample.
questions.hint: What happens in the period that does not fit?
